dedupe_keys.name: hanshin awaji 1995 and taiwan 1999 earthquakes comparison of emergency medical response and lessons for japan

description: This case study compares the emergency medical response to two major earthquakes: the Hanshin-Awaji (Kobe) earthquake of 1995 in Japan and the Taiwan earthquake of September 1999. Noboru Ishii and colleagues at Kobe University presented it as a conference abstract published in Prehospital and Disaster Medicine in 2000. They describe how Japan's system for disaster medical response was being rebuilt after the Kobe lessons and what the Taiwan response showed. In Taiwan, damage to local government offices was limited, so incident command could be unified; many severely injured patients were moved out of the disaster area; the army brought in large quantities of medical equipment; and medical teams from unaffected areas were dispatched quickly. Coverage is the two affected regions. The abstract is available online and free to read on Cambridge Core. Caveats: this is a short abstract without figures, and it reflects the authors' observations, not a systematic evaluation. The authors call for Japan to build rapid dispatch of search and rescue teams with medical teams, helicopter transfer of the severely injured to unaffected areas through core disaster hospitals, and coordination of multiple agencies. Simulation uses: response design options, such as patient evacuation by air and outside medical teams, for earthquake medical surge and evacuation models. Related records: the Nepal 2015 tertiary hospital resilience study (case_study-nepal-2015-earthquake-tertiary-hospital-resilience) and the post-earthquake hospital transportation model (model-post-earthquake-hospital-transportation-abm) address later earthquake responses.
